connections.label: Operação Prato (Operation Saucer)
connections.note: A file titled 'Operação Prato', written by the US journalist Bob Pratt, is served publicly in the MUFON/Pratt document set at documents.theblackvault.com. It opens: 'Operação Prato, a Brazilian Air Force investigation of a prolonged UFO flap in 1977-78'. It names Captain Uyrangê Hollanda and his six sergeants, names Brigadier Protázio Lopes de Oliveira as the Belém base commander who shut the operation down after four months, and describes the interviews of hundreds of witnesses in Colares and about thirty other villages. This is the concrete answer to whether Prato material reached US hands: it did, through a working reporter, and it is now in the same FOIA archive that carries the Elizondo and Grusch-era US paper.

He interviewed Captain Uyrange Hollanda, who had led the official investigation in the Colares region. Pratt was later able to secure brief summaries of 281 incidents in Colares and surrounding areas, plus maps, and twenty photographs.' Hollanda told him his team 'took about three hundred photos and we photographed eight different types of UFOs.' Tier 2: the interview and the 281 summaries are reported by a named researcher quoting Pratt's 1996 book, and the Pratt file at The Black Vault is the surviving public artefact of that chain.

desc: The Black Vault is the private FOIA archive through which the overwhelming majority of primary documents in this domain reached the public: the Elizondo resignation letters, the Garry Reid memoranda, the DD Form 1910, the Neill Tipton messaging emails, the Elizondo-Gough correspondence, the Army's denial of the TTSA CRADA correspondence, and the DoD Inspector General files. It is not aligned with the disclosure movement's conclusions and has publicly contested several of them, which is what gives its releases their evidentiary force — these are documents extracted by an adversarial requester, not supplied by an interested party.

dossier.narrative: The archive's place on this board is structural: it is the mechanism, not the argument. Two of the records opened in this corpus show why it earns a node rather than a footnote. The first is the 341st Strategic Missile Wing release of 14 June 2001, eighty-seven pages of excerpts from five quarterly wing histories, sent to Greenewald by HQ 341st Space Wing in answer to a request of 9 May 2001. That release is the document the board's Malmstrom node has always named as decisive, and it is the one that states the Air Force's own conclusion and withholds the engineering report behind it. The second is the Defense Intelligence Agency release of 22 August 1996, IR 6 846 0139 76 on the Tehran F-4 intercepts, with DIA's covering letter stating that a search of its systems of records located one document responsive to the subject of the request. Both are cases where what the government holds, and how little of it, is knowable only because somebody outside asked in writing and published the answer with its covering letter attached.
